clinicalPearls: A midline cyst arising from dilatation of the prostatic utricle, which opens into the prostatic urethra at the verumontanum
Strongly associated with genitourinary anomalies such as hypospadias, cryptorchidism, unilateral renal agenesis and disorders of sex development
It usually presents in childhood or adolescence, in contrast to mullerian duct cysts, which present later
Because it communicates with the urethra it may contain spermatozoa, unlike a mullerian duct cyst
It can cause recurrent urinary tract infection, post-void dribbling, epididymitis, stone formation within the cyst, or infertility
Voiding cystourethrography may show the cyst filling from the urethra, while MRI defines the surrounding anatomy
Small asymptomatic cysts are observed, whereas symptomatic ones may need transurethral or surgical treatment
reference.pathophysiology: The prostatic utricle is a small midline mullerian remnant that opens into the prostatic urethra at the verumontanum. Incomplete regression, often linked with under-virilisation, allows it to dilate into a cyst. Because it communicates with the urethra, urine can reflux into it, predisposing to stasis, infection and stone formation, and when spermatozoa enter it the cyst may contain sperm.
additionalDifferentials: Mullerian duct cyst, which has no urethral communication
Seminal vesicle cyst, which is laterally placed
additionalInvestigations: Voiding cystourethrography to demonstrate communication with the urethra
Pelvic MRI for midline anatomy and associated anomalies
Retrograde urethrography or urethroscopy to view the utricular opening
Renal tract imaging for associated anomalies
Assessment for disorders of sex development where indicated
redFlags: Recurrent infection, abscess or stone formation within the cyst
Association with disorders of sex development requiring endocrine and genetic evaluation
Obstructive symptoms or upper urinary tract compromise
Rare malignant change in long-standing cysts
reference.prognosis: Generally good; small cysts are asymptomatic and stable, while symptomatic utricle cysts respond to endoscopic or surgical treatment, although proximity to the ejaculatory ducts and continence structures requires care.
pitfalls: Confusing a utricle cyst, which communicates with the urethra and may contain sperm, with a mullerian duct cyst
Missing associated hypospadias, cryptorchidism, renal agenesis or a disorder of sex development
Damaging the ejaculatory ducts or continence mechanism during intervention
Overlooking the cyst as a cause of recurrent urinary tract infection or epididymitis in a boy
